I call to order the second meeting of the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention. Please delegates take your seats because I will now invite the Committee to continue its consideration of agenda item two entitled Effective implementation of the Convention at national, subregional and regional levels. The documents before the committee are listed in today's journal and in the app. We will turn to sub-item D entitled development and promotion of activities for targeted capacity building to further the implementation of the convention. I will now give the floor to a representative of the UNCCD secretariat to introduce the documents. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. Distinguished delegates, I have the honor to introduce document ICCD/CRC/24/3, which corresponds to the draft decision contained in chapter two of document ICCD/CRC/24/5. The document ICCD/CRC24/3 is entitled Promotion of Capacity Building to Further the Implementation of the Convention. Pursuant to decision two, COP16, the Secretariat in collaboration with the global mechanism and relevant partners have continued to implement targeted capacity building to support the effective implementation of the convention. Progress has been made in support of the 2026 national reporting process, the second phase of the land degradation neutrality target setting program, which is TSP 2.0, gender responsive capacity building under the gender action plan, and the expansion of digital tools, including the use of earth observation and artificial intelligence. The document reports on activities implemented by the secretariats and the global mechanism, as well as complementary efforts by the Group of 20 Global Land Initiative, or G20 GLI, which spans education outreach, technical cooperation, partnership-based capacity building, targeted support for national reporting, LDN TSB 2.0, drought, and other policy frameworks. Building on this official document, the committee will hold an interactive dialogue entitled Scaling Up Capacity Development for Transformative Change, providing a practical illustration through selected examples of capacity building in action. Contributions will be provided by the G20 GLI, the Global Policy Advocacy and Regional Cooperation Unit of the Secretariat and the Global Mechanism. Their presentations will be followed by an exchange with parties and observers. The dialogue aims to inform future priorities, delivery modalities, partnerships, the emerging capacity building strategy and the annual work program subject to the availability of resources. Madam Chair, distinguished delegates, I am joined on the podium by representatives of the G20 GLI, the Secretariat and the global mechanism who will contribute to this interactive dialogue. Thank you.
I think the representative of the UNCCD secretariat. I will now give the floor to Miss Wagaki Vishnevsky on the G20 Global Land Initiative.

Thank you, Chair. think I need the presentation, please. Thank you, Chair. So the G20 Global Land Initiative has a big mandate, which is to reduce degraded land by 50% by 2040. One of the things that has driven the work of the G20 Global Land Initiative in this regard is to scale resources in order to scale restoration. we're constantly reminded that we need to remember that scaling one, you know, restoration by a hectare or two is not sufficient. We have a billion hectares to restore by 2030 and half of that, I think by 2040. So we approach the work of capacity building, um, in three, in, in, in, in several areas, but I just will highlight a few for you to see the kind of work we've done. One of the things we realized is that we don't have enough graduates coming from universities that work with the land and that understand what land restoration is or exactly what we're doing. So we're looking at scaling the number of graduates or people coming from school that understand this issue. And so we have university courses that we've developed. We also recognized very early on that at the national level, a lot of the countries that have legislation at the national level on land restoration or land degradation, addressing land degradation, are able to implement faster than countries that have no legislation. And so we have developed a special academy called the Global Change Maker Academy for parliamentarians, where every year we're bringing them to understand to the academy where they're taught or they learn about the convention, its relation to other conventions and what restoration means and what kind of legislation is needed. But they also learn where the future is going in terms of how they need to think about legislation. That academy, by the way, is taking place alongside this COP next week. Third, we are looking at young people because for G20, the generation that will be here by 2040 is not us. We focus a lot on what we call Gen. Z, and they are at a very different place than where we are. And so we are looking at how do we engage them from where they stand. And so one of the things we've developed is something called the startups in land restoration, which has gained a lot of traction and which is actually happening at national level in many countries. The fourth thing we recognize in terms of government demand was the use of technology to map, to monitor what is happening on the ground. So we've developed a platform that enables us to provide that kind of monitoring with partners across the world that are able to support any country in the world that wishes to be involved or to use geospatial planning. And then the last thing we've recognized is the need for public outreach, because until the public buys into what we're doing, we're not going to make a big difference. What does that mean for capacity building? For us, we want to align restoration with what stakeholders want. And some of the things we have realized is land restoration has been happening very much on a voluntary basis, very much funded by governments in a way that there's no return. And what a lot of governments are looking for is to build economies, is to create jobs, is to optimize the resources they have. So a lot of the activities that we are doing are aimed at ensuring we can optimize resource use, whether we are using geospatial mapping to ensure that We can track where restoration is happening, where it could be happening faster, where the resources are being provided and where there are no resources. All of these things are able to be assessed using these tools. In terms of job centered youth, we have found that a lot of innovations are coming from young people, innovations that deal with problems that they are experiencing in their communities. So if you're looking at building capacity, we need to think what are the solutions that young people are bringing to the table and how can we support them? Because the biggest challenge for them has been once they identify a technology and once they identify a mechanism for actually changing that to make it usable, they don't have the resources to support it. The most important thing I would hope we take away today is that the young people are actually asking for new models of how we do business, new models of how we run the economy, and they're providing some of those solutions. But we then need to back up those solutions with support. So the startups that they're coming up with are solutions that address the needs that youth are asking for, but then we need as an institution to provide the mechanism and the environment for them to grow them. Lastly, we are looking at the restoration economy because we recognize that until land restoration provides a resource base and it becomes an income generating tool, it will not be very easy for the rest of the government sectors to kind of take on and support the initiatives that come under land restoration. The last thing that we are grappling with, and this is what my colleague will be speaking about, is artificial intelligence. And in this case, we're looking at artificial intelligence from two perspectives, in terms of it driving land restoration and how we can use it, but on the other hand, in terms of the AI land footprint. Chair, that is my presentation, thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, my colleague, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. As my colleague mentioned, I would like to delve on the question of artificial intelligence as it applies to land restoration, as it applies to capacity building. When we at the G20 Global Land Initiative started looking at the mandate which was given to us by the G20 which is to achieve 50% reduction in degraded land by 2040. We looked at the pool of human resources available to achieve this restoration. We looked at the commitments globally made by parties to achieve restoration. As of 2025, Parties are committed between various processes, the Bonn Challenge, the LDN process, the CBD process and UNFCCC process, 1.2 billion hectares of land to be restored. But when you look at the pool of experts available to do this, we are looking at something like 10,000 experts globally. The largest network of restoration professionals is still less than 10,000. Now, you cannot achieve 1.2 billion hectares of land to be restored with a pool of 10,000 restoration specialists. That's why we decided to scale at an absolutely massive scale, going initially to the university where land is a subject matter of discussion, such as agricultural universities, such as urban planning universities, such as mining universities, such as forestry universities. Wherever land is a domain of their learning, we are injecting those university curriculum. As we speak, we have already reached out to more than 1,200 universities. 600 of them has already started teaching land restoration from a curriculum which we have trained. We are currently working the massive open courses, online courses, working with the UN University to scale it to a million graduates outside the university system. We are going to work with major providers such as Coursera to make this training available free of cost to the community, be it government or private sector. It is in this context that we are looking at the question of artificial intelligence. We understand that at this point of time, artificial intelligence is a very hot topic and there are many concerns among people, including environmental concern. Artificial intelligence and data centers are causing huge energy footprint. It is causing huge water footprint, but it's also caused causing huge land footprint in three levels. The land needed for the data centers is most obvious, but that's the smallest of the footprint. The land being mined to create the critical minerals which go into the memory chips which go into the data centers is much bigger. Now there is a commitment from major AI companies that renewable energy will be used for data centers, which then could expand the footprint of land much beyond the data centers themselves. So we are currently embarking on a collaborative project with the International Telecommunication Union, with the International Renewable Energy Agency, the United Nations University, to first of all understand how land footprint is involved in AI, but also then build capacity within national governments to integrate it as a part of their national environmental impact assessment process. So that when a data center is being proposed, the national agencies should be able to do a lifecycle analysis of the land footprint of the AI and the data centers. We would of course make this available also to the civil society and also to the industry so that they can also do their own analysis. So this is one segment of AI. The second segment of AI is how can we use AI in assessing land restoration? We are now developing a model. As I said, we have 1.2 billion hectares of land which parties are already committed to restore. How do we prioritize? Where is the best bang for buck? What technologies could be used in which locations? And there is tremendous potential of the use of artificial intelligence. Working with UNEP and the Global Resource Information Directorate in Geneva, we have looked at how abandoned mining sites can be captured by machine learning so that we can identify those sites which can be restored as a matter of priority. Once again, we want to scale it globally and bring this approach to the parties, to the civil society and to the restoration economy. And finally, We also believe that AI itself can be a tool for capacity building. In addition to training experts, human beings, in the parties in civil society and the industry, there is also a potential to create AI agents who themselves can be the experts to support each of these above parties. So currently we are working on developing such AI agents who can be used, who can be trained with the best of the technology, who can be trained in specific domains, who can be deployed at scale, who can be deployed in multiple languages, who can be constantly updated, almost updated in real time. With this combined effort of training AI agents and deploying it at scale, we expect that we will be able to bring the best of the knowledge to desktop and the mobiles of every person who need that information in real time. Thank you.
